question: Can Muslims congratulate non-Muslims on their religious holidays or say Merry Christmas back?
asked: What should I do if my colleague passes by me and says Merry Christmas to me? What should I do if they greet me with Merry Christmas?
answer:
As for congratulating them, this is a much more detailed question. I'm going to summarize it. Maybe one day I'll give a longer answer, and I have given a longer lecture; you will find it online. But to summarize: there is nothing explicit in the Qur'an or the Sunnah, or any of the four Imams, or any of the early scholars in this regard.

One of the earliest scholars to have a detailed discussion about this is Ibn al-Qayyim, in his famous book *Ahkam Ahl al-Dhimmah*, or the rulings of the people of dhimmah. And he made a very famous remark there, which is now well known and a lot of people quote, in which he very, very strongly prohibited congratulating the non-Muslims on their holy days, on their days of celebration. And he said a phrase here: to congratulate them on their holy days is worse than congratulating them for a major sin, like drinking alcohol or like murder. So he is saying to congratulate them on their holy day, because of their holy day, is a bigger sin than to congratulate them for a sin that they do.

Now, by the way, because of this, because people don't read Arabic or don't understand it, some neophyte said in a lecture that to say Merry Christmas is worse than murder, and that this is the position of Ibn al-Qayyim. And nothing could be further from the truth. And this guy's video went viral, the right took hold of it, and this and that. You don't understand fiqh and usul al-fiqh and 'aqidah, and you start giving fatwas; this is what happens. Ibn al-Qayyim never said that. Ibn al-Qayyim said what I had explained.

And even that is one opinion. And I respect that opinion; he is a great scholar, he has the right to say that. But that is one opinion; there are other opinions as well. And if you look at the fatawa of so many modern councils, the European Council of Fatwa and so many, they disagree with this fatwa. And the reason is very simple. See, here's the 'illah, here is the cause. When you congratulate somebody for their holy day, do you mean to congratulate them for worshipping other than Allah? If you do, then Ibn al-Qayyim's fatwa is in its place. If your intention, or if your paradigm, is that, "Yes, you're worshipping other than Allah. Yes, good, mabruk to that, congratulations, more power to you," then Ibn al-Qayyim's fatwa is 110% accurate. How can you congratulate somebody for worshipping other than Allah?

But see, here's the point. When you say congratulatory phrases, positive phrases, is that what is implied? That is the issue of controversy between Ibn al-Qayyim and many other scholars of our times. When you go and you say some generic greeting, even if you say the phrase "Merry Christmas" back unto you, if he comes and says "Merry Christmas" and then you say, "Oh, Merry Christmas to you as well," even though I'm going to say at the end that we shouldn't say that, but I'm saying even if you said it, blunt question: in the context that we live in, will anybody understand from you that you are congratulating them for worshipping other than Allah? Is this the understanding of the phrase? No. What is the understanding? Just a greeting. And this is the paradigm of so many other 'ulama of our times.

By the way, you will find very little classical discussion on this, only a few. And also this must be said: most of these fatawa are in the context of a Muslim-dominant Islamic land, where the dynamics are very different. And one needs to ask, why would a Muslim land be celebrating Christmas? Of course you should be ultra strict, etc., etc. None of these fatawa deal with minorities, until modern times. So in my humble opinion, even to quote Ibn Taymiyyah, copy and paste, and apply it to America or Europe is in itself a mistake, because the fatwa of Ibn Taymiyyah is a different context, different time, different place. And even then, it is one opinion.

Nonetheless, there are a whole host of 'ulama in our times who have said that it is permissible to generically greet. And I personally say: get out of the controversy and do not say the words "Merry Christmas." This is my personal advice. Rather, when somebody comes and says "Merry Christmas" to you, say something generic in response: "God bless you." God bless you, generic. May Allah bless you with hidayah, with iman, with Islam, with good health. You can make du'a for the non-Muslim, right? "God bless you," or something generic of this nature. There should be nothing wrong with this.

Allah says in the Qur'an: when somebody comes and greets you, greet him back with a better greeting, or at least return the same greeting. This is a generic verse. So somebody says "Good morning," you say "Good morning to you as well." Somebody says "Good afternoon," "Good afternoon to you as well." Somebody says "Merry Christmas": in my humble opinion, even though I do not say it is haram, by the way, I want to be very clear, still, just to get out of the controversy, **don't say back "Merry Christmas"; just say "May God bless you," "God bless," or "Happy seasons," or something of this nature.**

And to conclude this question: Ibn 'Abbas said, if Fir'awn said to me "Rahimakallah," I would say, "May Allah have mercy on you as well." If Fir'awn were to make a du'a for me, I would say back unto you, may Allah also have mercy on you. What's wrong? Meaning, if Fir'awn were alive and he said this to me, why can't I respond, even to Fir'awn, with a similar thing? So there's nothing wrong with giving a generic response back, and it does not imply any type of servitude to other than Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.
